lesson.title: Measuring Frequency: Reading It Off the Screen, One Way or Another
lesson.summary: The most direct way to measure a repeating signal's frequency is to read its period off an oscilloscope's timebase and take the reciprocal, though a spectrum analyzer can also show frequency directly as the position of a peak along its horizontal axis.
lesson.body:
You already know the relationship between period and frequency, they are reciprocals of each other, and you have already seen how to read a period directly off an oscilloscope screen by counting horizontal divisions for one full cycle and multiplying by the time/div setting. Frequency measurement, in the most common case, is simply that same process followed by one extra step: once you have the period, invert it to get the frequency in hertz.

Take a fresh example to make the arithmetic concrete. Suppose the oscilloscope's time/div control is set to 20 milliseconds per division, and one complete cycle of the waveform on screen spans 2.5 horizontal divisions. The period is T = 2.5 times 20 ms = 50 ms, or 0.050 seconds. The frequency is then f = 1/T = 1/0.050 = 20 Hz. Notice that the oscilloscope never displayed a frequency number at all; it displayed a shape, and you extracted the period from that shape and calculated the frequency yourself, exactly as before with the 100 Hz example.

There is a second way to read frequency, one that does not require measuring a period at all: a spectrum analyzer displays amplitude against frequency directly, so the fundamental frequency of a signal simply appears as the position of its tallest peak along the horizontal axis, no calculation needed. This becomes especially convenient for a signal with a messy or hard to read time domain shape, where picking a clean start and end point for one cycle on an oscilloscope is difficult, but the fundamental frequency still stands out clearly as a single dominant peak on a spectrum analyzer.
